text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- A state working group said the government should consider making it illegal to buy or be in possession of bootleg alcohol just as it is illegal to make or sell it. A study found that over half of all 16 year olds had drunk black market alcohol and tightening up the laws could cut down this consumption.

- Central bank governor Urban Backstrom says a quick link to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) would be counter productive. He siad there must be strong public support for the move and as this has not been achieved there has been no contact with other European central banks to discuss a possible link even though Sweden's economy is ready.
- Violence among children and teenagers is increasing in line with a rise in the general community. A study by Save The Children found up to nine percent of children are bullied at school.

- Helplines for new Internet subscribers were swamped at Christmas with every new owner ringing on average twice to get help with connection. The newspaper had trouble getting through to Telia's helpline and Tele2 had a five minutes wait.

- The first step in toolmaker Sandvik's concentration in the Russian market is made with the company's purchase of Russia's biggest hard metal workshop MKTS. Sandvik is investing 300 million crown over three years in MKTS and is optimistic for the future, says managing director Clas Ake Hedstrom.

- IT shares could be the losers of 1997 after coming out tops this year. Companies like Lap Power, WM-data, and IBS are being put on sell recommendations by many of the 100 Swedish brokers and analysts surveyed by the paper alongside Hennes & Mauritz, MoDo, and Volvo. Recommended stocks were Astra, Incentive, and S-E-Banken.

- Finance Minister Erik Asbrink is optimistic for 1997, expecting more rate cuts, stronger growth and lower unemployment. In an interview he said the sale of the state's holding of Nordbanken would be conducted on its own merits and he did not have strong support for any particular bidder.
- Eight top women have left SAS in the past year for other leading jobs. The majority of them have cited the new company culture with a closed doors attitude as a reason for leaving.
